canonical_statement: The trial evaluated the effectiveness and safety of providing multiple as-needed doses of oral ondansetron after emergency-department discharge to children with acute gastroenteritis-associated vomiting.
Investigators conducted a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled superiority trial at six Canadian tertiary-care pediatric emergency departments.

Eligible children were 6 months to less than 18 years old, had acute gastroenteritis, at least three vomiting episodes in the preceding 24 hours, symptom onset less than 72 hours earlier, vomiting within 6 hours before enrollment, and had received ondansetron in the emergency department.

population.label: Children 6 months to <18 years with acute gastroenteritis-associated vomiting after receiving ondansetron in a pediatric emergency department
inclusion_criteria: At least 3 vomiting episodes in prior 24 hours
Received ondansetron in the emergency department

canonical_statement: Key exclusions included hematemesis or bilious vomiting, specified cardiac/QT risks, complex congenital heart disease, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and use of specified QT-prolonging, serotonergic, neuroleptic, electrolyte-altering, or other 5-HT3-antagonist medications.

population.label: Children 6 months to <18 years with acute gastroenteritis-associated vomiting after receiving ondansetron in a pediatric emergency department
exclusion_criteria: Long-QT syndrome or ventricular arrhythmia history in participant or first-degree relative

canonical_statement: Randomization was 1:1 using random block sizes of 4 and 6, stratified by site and weight below versus at least 20 kg; participants, trial and clinical staff, and data analysts were unaware of assignments.

Caregivers received oral ondansetron solution for up to six doses at 0.15 mg/kg per dose (maximum 8 mg), administered as needed for ongoing vomiting or nausea no more often than every 8 hours during the first 48 hours after enrollment.

canonical_statement: Caregiver follow-up occurred at 24 hours, 48 hours, and day 7 and captured symptoms, health-care use, study medication administration, and adverse events.

The primary outcome was moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis during the 7 days after enrollment, defined as a modified Vesikari Scale score of at least 9 using only postrandomization symptoms and events.

outcome.definition: Modified Vesikari Scale score >=9; score range 0-20; only postrandomization symptoms/events included

canonical_statement: Prespecified secondary outcomes included presence and duration of vomiting, number of vomiting episodes within 48 hours, unscheduled health-care visits within 7 days, intravenous fluid receipt within 7 days, and caregiver satisfaction at day 7.

outcome.definition: Vomiting presence/duration/frequency, unscheduled health care, IV fluids, and caregiver satisfaction

canonical_statement: The trial was designed for 90% power to detect a 10-percentage-point absolute reduction in the primary outcome; no interim analyses of primary or secondary outcomes were planned, and Holm adjustment controlled family-wise error for secondary outcomes and interaction tests.

Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle, used multiple imputation for missing regression-analysis data, and adjusted secondary outcomes for trial site and weight category using prespecified models.
A total of 1030 participants underwent randomization: 517 were assigned to ondansetron, 512 to placebo, and one was not assigned because of a website error.

canonical_statement: Daily follow-up occurred only for the first 2 days, while the subsequent 5 days were summarized in a single survey, so recall bias could not be ruled out.
Treatment effects on the composite modified Vesikari outcome require cautious interpretation even though the scale has been validated and used in similar studies.

Because the trial was conducted in Canadian emergency departments and the outcome included subsequent health-care visits and treatments, findings should be interpreted in the context of local health-care-use patterns.
The authors concluded that providing ondansetron after an emergency-department visit for recent and frequent gastroenteritis-associated vomiting was beneficial.
The authors supported providing a small number of doses (for example, two) to patients with symptoms that would have met trial eligibility, rather than routinely providing a large multidose supply.

The trial was supported by a Canadian Institutes of Health Research Strategy for Patient-Oriented Research Innovative Clinical Trials Initiative multiyear grant and multiple participating research institutions; Dr. Freedman also received a named professorship.
The article states that a data-sharing statement is available with the full text at NEJM.org.

The final protocol (version 4.0, 25 November 2022) allowed a generic oral ondansetron product to substitute when brand-name Zofran was unavailable because of intermittent supply issues, with a matching placebo formulation update.
